title: Approximation and Estimation
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Approximation and Estimation. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Estimate and exact value

Estimation replaces difficult values with nearby convenient numbers to predict a result or check whether an exact answer is reasonable. Rounding has a stated precision; an estimate is usually not exact. For products, choose rounded factors that are easy to multiply; for division, use compatible numerator and denominator values.

Bounds and error

If a positive value rounds to a to the nearest unit u, the original value is within half a unit of a, subject to the tie convention. Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference from the exact value. Relative error compares that error with the exact value. Keeping more significant figures generally gives a tighter approximation.

Worked example: (\(49.8 \times 20.2\)) is close to (\(50 \times 20=1,000\)). The exact result is 1,005.96, so the estimate has the right scale and is a useful check.

Choosing precision

Keep guard digits while calculating and round only the final result unless the question says otherwise. If options are far apart, a rough estimate may eliminate choices. If options are close, use exact arithmetic or bounds rather than rounding too early.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Round one factor up and another down when that balances a product estimate.
  • For a percentage, estimate the base value first; 10% is one tenth.
  • Use the first nonzero digit to compare orders of magnitude.
  • When a choice is near a rounding boundary, calculate exactly or bound it.
  • Keep units and precision consistent in measurement and money problems.

Common traps

  • Repeatedly rounding intermediate results can accumulate error.
  • More decimal places do not mean more accuracy when input measurements are approximate.
  • Use an approximation symbol or words such as about; do not present an estimate as exact.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Nearest unit u: rounding error is at most u/2.
  • Significant figures start at the first nonzero digit.
  • Estimate first, but compute exactly when the question or close options require it.
  • Check sign, units and order of magnitude.
  • Round intermediate values only when explicitly instructed.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    Which is the best estimate of (\(398\times5.1\))?

    1. (\(200\))
    2. (\(2,000\))
    3. (\(20,000\))
    4. (\(400\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(2,000\))

    Round (\(398\approx400\)) and (\(5.1\approx5\)). Then (\(400\times5=2,000\)).

  2. Core:

    To the nearest ten, what is (\(1,246\))?

    1. (\(1,240\))
    2. (\(1,245\))
    3. (\(1,250\))
    4. (\(1,200\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1,250\))

    The ones digit is 6, so round the tens digit up: (\(1,246\approx1,250\)).

  3. Foundation:

    Round (\(6,847\)) to the nearest hundred.

    1. (\(6,800\))
    2. (\(6,840\))
    3. (\(6,850\))
    4. (\(6,900\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6,800\))

    The tens digit is 4, so the hundreds digit stays unchanged: 6,847 rounds to 6,800.

  4. Standard:

    Which is the best estimate of (\(19.8 \times 0.49\))?

    1. (\(1\))
    2. (\(10\))
    3. (\(100\))
    4. (\(1,000\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(10\))

    Use (\(20 \times 0.5=10\)). The exact product is close to 10.

  5. Challenge:

    Which value rounds to (\(8.4 cm\)) to the nearest tenth under the usual half-up rule?

    1. (\(8.34 cm\))
    2. (\(8.41 cm\))
    3. (\(8.46 cm\))
    4. (\(8.51 cm\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(8.41 cm\))

    Values from 8.35 cm up to but not including 8.45 cm round to 8.4 cm. Only 8.41 cm is in that interval.
